summary: Fine-tuning makes sense when you need to change a model's behavior, style, or format consistently, encode domain knowledge or specialized vocabulary into model weights, or reduce latency/cost by shrinking prompts — all cases where in-context examples alone are insufficient. RAG is the better choice when your knowledge is dynamic, fact-heavy, or needs citations, while prompt engineering should always be your first and cheapest experiment. In practice, teams often combine a fine-tuned model with RAG rather than treating them as mutually exclusive.
when_to_fine_tune: Choose fine-tuning when you need consistent output structure, tone, or task-specific behavior that few-shot prompting can't reliably enforce.
Use it for domain adaptation when specialized terminology or reasoning patterns (e.g. legal, medical, code) are poorly represented in the base model.
Fine-tune to cut inference cost and latency by baking instructions into weights so you can use shorter prompts or smaller models.
Prefer RAG over fine-tuning when the underlying knowledge changes frequently or must be grounded in verifiable, citable sources.
